etymology: English surname Hooker, from an occupational or topographical root; the given name Thomas from the Aramaic t’oma, “twin.”
biblical_def: Thomas Hooker (1586–1647) was a Puritan divine of surpassing power in the pulpit, driven out of England by Archbishop Laud and settled at last in the New England wilderness, where he led his flock overland to found the colony of Connecticut. A preacher who searched the conscience without mercy and then poured in the balm of the gospel, he is best remembered for that great treatise on conversion, The Application of Redemption, in which he traced how the Spirit humbles a sinner, breaks the proud heart, and draws it home to Christ. Hooker would not let a man rest upon a shallow or presumptuous faith; he pressed contrition and true humiliation, that the soul might feel its bondage before it prized its Deliverer. Yet he was no gloomy legalist, for all his sharpness of application aimed at magnifying free grace, teaching that the same LORD who wounds also heals, and that the vilest sinner brought low may look to the crucified Redeemer and live. His labours planted a commonwealth ordered by covenant, and his sermons nourished a generation in the doctrines of grace. In him the New England way found one of its truest voices: a shepherd who fed the sheep, guarded the flock, and pointed every trembling seeker to the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of the world.
webster_summary: Puritan founder of Connecticut and preacher of the application of redemption.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the biblical order of salvation, wherein the LORD first empties before He fills, first slays the sinner’s self-righteousness before He clothes him in the righteousness of Christ. Where our day preaches an easy assurance without conviction, Hooker calls the church back to a faith that has counted its bondage and fled to the Redeemer.

etymology: English surname Cotton, from Old English cot-tūn, a settlement or homestead; the given name John from the Hebrew Yōhānān, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Cotton (1585–1652) was the learned teacher of the church in Boston and, more than any other, the theological conscience of early New England. Trained at Cambridge and long a preacher in old Boston in Lincolnshire, he came at last to the new Boston across the sea, where his ministry so shaped the colony that it was said he could shape the church-order of a commonwealth by a single sermon. He wrote Milk for Babes, a plain catechism that fed the children of the covenant upon the first principles of the oracles of God, teaching the little ones their sin, their Saviour, and their duty. A man mighty in the Scriptures and warm in his exaltation of free grace, Cotton laboured that the church might be gathered of visible saints, bound by covenant, and governed by the Word alone. He prized the sovereignty of God in salvation and preached Christ as the whole of the gospel, so that even amid the controversies of his day his aim was ever to keep the Bride looking to her Bridegroom. In him the New England way found a teacher who joined depth of learning to plainness of speech, feeding both the strong and the weak, and pointing the rising generation to the LORD who is gracious.
webster_summary: Teacher of the Boston church and catechist of New England’s covenant children.

etymology: English surname Eliot, a diminutive form of Elias/Elijah, from the Hebrew 'Eliyyāhū, “my God is the LORD”; the given name John from Yōhānān, “the LORD is gracious.”
biblical_def: John Eliot (1604–1690), pastor of Roxbury in the Massachusetts colony, is honoured across the ages as “the Apostle to the Indians.” Not content to shepherd his English flock, he burned with compassion for the native peoples of New England, and he gave the strength of his long life to bring them the gospel of Jesus Christ. He learned their difficult Algonquin tongue, gathered converts into “praying towns” ordered by the Word of God, and above all laboured to render the whole Scripture into their language—the first complete Bible printed in the New World was Eliot’s Algonquin translation, a monument of patience and love. He counted no toil too great, no journey too hard, that a people sitting in darkness might see the great light. In this he walked in the footsteps of the apostles, obeying the great commission to disciple the nations, and testifying that the LORD is gracious to gather His elect out of every kindred and tongue. Eliot’s missionary zeal rebukes every parochial faith that hoards the gospel; his translation-labour honours the truth that the Word must be given to men in their own speech, that they may hear in their own language the wonderful works of God. His name stands with those who counted not their lives dear, that Christ might be preached to the ends of the earth.
webster_summary: The Apostle to the Indians, who translated the whole Bible into Algonquin.

etymology: English given name Edward, from Old English Eadweard, “rich guardian” or “blessed protector”; the surname Payson, a patronymic form, “son of Pay,” a medieval English personal name.
biblical_def: Edward Payson (1783–1827), pastor of the Second Church in Portland in the district of Maine, was so given to intercession that he is remembered by the church as “Praying Payson.” Though he ministered but a short span and died young, worn out in his Master’s service, his life burned with an ardour of communion with God that has kindled generations since. He wrestled in secret prayer until, it was said, the very boards of his study floor were worn where he knelt; and out of that hidden fellowship he came forth into the pulpit clothed with power, preaching Christ crucified with a tenderness and a nearness to heaven that melted his hearers. On his deathbed, racked with pain, he yet overflowed with such joy in the LORD that his dying testimonies were gathered up and treasured as a legacy of assurance and holy triumph. Payson teaches the church that the strength of a ministry is drawn from the closet, that no eloquence can supply the want of prayer, and that the man who would move his people Godward must first prevail with God for them. His life is a standing rebuke to prayerless labour and a sweet encouragement that the LORD hears the fervent cry of His servants, and crowns a praying ministry with fruit and with joy unspeakable and full of glory.
webster_summary: The Maine pastor called “Praying Payson” for his ardour in secret intercession.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is importunate, secret prayer as the wellspring of all faithful labour. Where our busy age prizes method and machinery, Payson calls the servant of Christ back to the worn floorboards of the study, to prevail with God before he presumes to prevail with men, that his dying hour may overflow, as his did, with joy unspeakable.

etymology: The given name Ashbel from the Hebrew, a name in the tribe of Benjamin (Gen 46:21), commonly rendered “man of Baal” or “flowing”; the surname Green, an English topographical name from the village green.
biblical_def: Ashbel Green (1762–1848) was a Presbyterian minister of the old school, chaplain to the Congress of the young republic, pastor in Philadelphia, and afterward president of the College of New Jersey at Princeton. A son of the manse and a soldier’s son who had seen the Revolution, he gave his mature years to the sober cause of orthodox learning and the training of a godly ministry. As president he laboured to keep the college anchored in vital piety and sound Reformed doctrine, grieving over the coldness of the times and pleading for genuine religion among the young men committed to his charge; under his hand a revival visited the college, to his lasting joy. He was afterward a chief mover in the founding of Princeton Theological Seminary, that the church might have a fountain of learned and orthodox pastors, and he presided long over its board. A man of firm principle and unbending fidelity to the Westminster standards, Green stood in the gap for confessional Presbyterianism in an age of drift. His life witnesses that the health of the church depends upon the sound instruction of her ministers, and that Christian learning is no enemy but a handmaid to true piety. He served his generation by the will of God, guarding the deposit and passing it faithfully to those who came after.
webster_summary: Old-school Presbyterian, president of Princeton, and founder of Princeton Seminary.

etymology: The given name Samuel from the Hebrew Sh'mū'ēl, “asked of God” or “heard of God”; the surname Miller, an English occupational name for one who grinds grain.
biblical_def: Samuel Miller (1769–1850) was the second professor of Princeton Theological Seminary, a Presbyterian divine of wide learning and settled orthodoxy who taught church history and government to a generation of American pastors. Standing alongside Archibald Alexander at the founding of the seminary, he gave nearly four decades to the training of ministers in the old Reformed and Presbyterian way. Miller is especially remembered for his careful writing upon the office of the ruling elder, in which he defended from Scripture the twofold eldership of the church—those who labour in the word and doctrine, and those who rule—and vindicated Presbyterian government as the pattern given by the apostles. He held that Christ has set officers in His church for her order, edification, and defence, and that the ruling elder shares with the pastor in oversight, discipline, and the care of souls. A man of dignity, prayer, and firm principle, Miller stood for confessional fidelity against the innovations of his time. His labours upon the eldership continue to instruct the church in her government, reminding her that the shepherding of Christ’s flock is committed not to one man alone but to a plurality of elders who must watch for souls as they that must give account. In Miller the Princeton tradition found a churchman as well as a scholar, guarding both the doctrine and the order of the house of God.
webster_summary: Princeton Seminary professor and expounder of the office of the ruling elder.

Where our age tends either to one-man rule or to formless democracy, Miller calls the church to the apostolic order of qualified elders who must give account for those over whom the Holy Ghost has made them overseers.

etymology: The given name James from the Hebrew Ya'aqōv, “supplanter” (Jacob); Henley, an English place-name, “high wood or clearing”; Thornwell, an English topographical surname, “the well by the thorn.”
biblical_def: James Henley Thornwell (1812–1862) was among the ablest theologians the Southern Presbyterian church produced, a professor at Columbia and at South Carolina College, and a churchman of towering intellect and burning conviction. Rising from poverty to eminence, he devoted his powers to the defense of confessional Calvinism, the spirituality of the church, and the divine warrant of Presbyterian government. He held with unbending firmness that the church is a spiritual body with a spiritual mission, whose charter is the Word of God alone, and that whatsoever Christ has not commanded in her worship and order is forbidden—the regulative principle held with rare consistency. A preacher of great eloquence and searching power, he magnified the sovereignty of God, the ruin of man in sin, and the free grace of the covenant. Thornwell’s writings on church polity and the headship of Christ over His church remain a rich vein for those who would understand the crown rights of the Redeemer. Though he died on the eve of great sorrows for his region, his labours upon the constitution of the church and the doctrines of grace outlived him. He teaches the church to prize her spiritual character, to submit her worship and government wholly to the Word, and to own no King in Zion but the Lord Jesus Christ, who alone is Head over all things to His body.
webster_summary: Southern Presbyterian theologian of the spirituality of the church and Christ’s headship.

The principle to recover is the spirituality of the church and the crown rights of the Redeemer—that Christ’s kingdom is not of this world, and His church must worship and be governed only as He has commanded. Where our age would either secularize the church into a political engine or loosen her worship to human invention, Thornwell calls her back to the regulative principle and to the sole headship of the Lord Jesus in Zion.

etymology: The given name John from the Hebrew Yōhānān, “the LORD is gracious”; the surname Girardeau, of French Huguenot origin, a diminutive of Gérard, “brave with the spear.”
biblical_def: John Lafayette Girardeau (1825–1898), of Huguenot descent and Southern Presbyterian conviction, is remembered as a preacher of extraordinary power who gave the strength of his early ministry to the gospel among the enslaved of Charleston. At the Zion Church he gathered a great congregation of black worshippers, labouring among them with such fervour and such evident love that revival attended his preaching, and multitudes professed faith in Christ. He held that the gospel is for every soul without distinction, and that the Redeemer purchased worshippers out of every people; and he counted it no small part of his calling to bring the riches of Reformed truth to the poor and the bond. Afterward he became professor of theology at Columbia Seminary, where his lectures upon the doctrines of grace, the work of the Spirit, and the freedom of the will defended the old Calvinism against Arminian and rationalist error. A man of deep piety and mighty in prayer, Girardeau joined the passion of an evangelist to the precision of a theologian. His life witnesses that sovereign grace stoops to the lowliest, that the gospel levels every earthly rank before the cross, and that the same Spirit who quickens the mighty quickens the humble. He teaches the church to preach Christ freely to all, honouring in every hearer a soul for whom the Saviour shed His precious blood.

etymology: The given name Benjamin from the Hebrew Binyāmīn, “son of the right hand”; Morgan, a Welsh name, “sea-born” or “sea-circle”; the surname Palmer, from a medieval pilgrim who bore a palm from the Holy Land.
biblical_def: Benjamin Morgan Palmer (1818–1902), long the pastor of the First Presbyterian Church in New Orleans, was the first moderator of the General Assembly of the Southern Presbyterian church and one of the most beloved preachers of his generation. A man of stately eloquence and pastoral tenderness, he laboured in New Orleans through war, pestilence, and yellow fever, refusing to flee his post when the plague swept the city, but staying to comfort the dying and bury the dead. He preached the sovereignty of God and the covenant of grace with a warmth that bound his people to him for a lifetime, and his ministry outlasted every calamity that befell his beloved city. Palmer held fast the confessional standards of the church and the spirituality of her mission, standing with Thornwell and the old Southern divines in vindicating the crown rights of the Redeemer. His printed sermons and his great work on family religion nourished the households of the church in covenant piety. Palmer teaches the shepherd to love his flock unto death, to abide at his post when others flee, and to feed the people upon the sovereign mercy of God through every darkness. His long and faithful ministry stands as a monument to constancy—a pastor who, having served his own generation by the will of God, fell asleep full of days and full of honour, mourned by a whole city.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry is preserved to honour a pastor whose lifelong constancy still commends the shepherd’s office. Palmer abode with his flock through plague and war, feeding a whole city upon the sovereign mercy of God and refusing to flee when the good shepherd’s duty was to stay.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is pastoral constancy and covenant household piety—the shepherd who loves his flock unto death and the family altar that nourishes the church. Where our age prizes mobility and ease, Palmer calls the minister to abide at his post through darkness, and calls the household to serve the LORD together, saying with Joshua, “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”

etymology: The given name Walter, from the Old High German Waltheri, “ruler of the army”; the surname Marshall, from the Old French mareschal, originally a keeper of horses, afterward a high officer.
biblical_def: Walter Marshall (1628–1680) was an English Puritan divine whose single enduring work, The Gospel Mystery of Sanctification, has fed the Reformed church for centuries and shaped the American Reformed understanding of holy living. Long troubled in his own soul, labouring after holiness under a legal spirit and finding no rest, Marshall came at last to the great discovery that sanctification, no less than justification, flows from union with Christ and is received by faith. He taught that the believer must first be assured of God’s free love in Christ before he can truly obey, that holiness is not the ground but the fruit of acceptance, and that the Spirit works true obedience by drawing the soul to rest wholly upon the Saviour. Against every legal striving that would build holiness upon the self, Marshall directed the weary to the fountain of grace, showing that we are sanctified by the very faith through which we are justified, and that Christ is made unto us not only righteousness but sanctification. His book unlocked the door of gospel obedience for multitudes bound in bondage, and it remains a chief treatise on how the believer, united to Christ, brings forth the fruits of a holy life. Marshall teaches the church that the way to holiness runs through the gospel, and that only they who rest in Christ’s finished work are set free to walk in newness of life.
